title: Processes (how life works)
summary: Step-by-step walkthroughs of the key processes of life.

layers.basics: Many biological ideas are really stories with a sequence of steps. This section lines them up so you can watch them unfold, from copying DNA to building an embryo.
layers.deeper: Each walkthrough lists steps in the order they usually happen. Most real processes overlap in time and are regulated, so the order is a teaching simplification. Some processes, such as the nitrogen cycle or speciation, still have open research questions, shown on their own cards.
layers.expert: Processes are summaries of branching, regulated, noisy networks; steps shown are the canonical pathway.

title: DNA replication
summary: Copying the genome before cell division.

layers.basics: The cell unzips its DNA and builds a new partner strand for each old strand, so two identical double helices result.
layers.deeper: Replication starts at origins, runs in both directions, and is checked for mistakes as it goes.
layers.expert: Fork speed ≈ 1,000 nt/s (E. coli) or ≈ 50 nt/s (human); error rate ≈ 10⁻⁹–10⁻¹⁰ per base after proofreading and mismatch repair.

facts: ≈ 25,000–50,000 initiation events estimated per S phase; mapping methods list from ≈ 25,000 to ≈ 250,000 candidate origin sites, and only a fraction fire in a given cell

steps.title: Origin recognition
steps.text: Initiator proteins bind an origin of replication and load the helicase.

steps.title: Unwinding
steps.text: Helicase separates the two strands, forming two replication forks; single-strand binding proteins and topoisomerase relieve strain.

steps.title: Priming
steps.text: Primase lays down short RNA primers to give DNA polymerase a starting point.

steps.title: Leading strand
steps.text: DNA polymerase extends the new strand continuously in the 5′→3′ direction towards the fork.

steps.title: Lagging strand
steps.text: The other strand is made in Okazaki fragments, each needing a primer.

steps.title: Joining and proofreading
steps.text: Primers are replaced, ligase seals nicks and proofreading and mismatch repair correct errors.

title: Transcription

layers.basics: RNA polymerase reads one strand of DNA and builds a matching RNA molecule.
layers.deeper: In eukaryotes the new RNA is capped, spliced and tailed before it leaves the nucleus.
layers.expert: Pol II elongates ≈ 1–4 kb/min; the Pol II CTD coordinates RNA processing. Bacterial transcription and translation are coupled.

facts: ≈ 25–30 bp upstream of the start in mammals; only a minority of human promoters have one (about a quarter have a TATA-like element, and only about a tenth of those, so a few percent overall, match the canonical TATAWAWR box)

steps.title: Initiation
steps.text: Transcription factors and RNA polymerase assemble at the promoter.

steps.title: Promoter opening
steps.text: The DNA is opened to a bubble of ≈ 12–14 bp and the template strand enters the polymerase.

steps.title: Elongation
steps.text: The polymerase adds ribonucleotides complementary to the template, 5′→3′.

steps.title: Termination
steps.text: In bacteria, a terminator sequence or the Rho protein makes the polymerase release the RNA and DNA. In eukaryotes, Pol II terminates downstream of the poly-A signal, and cleavage and poly-A addition at the 3′ end are coupled to this.

steps.title: Capping and polyadenylation
steps.text: A 5′ cap is added early, while the RNA is still being made. A poly-A tail is added at the 3′ end after the RNA is cleaved.

steps.title: Splicing and export
steps.text: The spliceosome removes introns, mostly while transcription is still under way; the mature mRNA exits through nuclear pores.

title: Glycolysis (steps)
summary: Ten steps from glucose to pyruvate.

layers.basics: One glucose is split in two halves with a small net profit of ATP and NADH.
layers.deeper: It has an investment phase (uses 2 ATP) and a payoff phase (makes 4 ATP and 2 NADH).
layers.expert: PFK-1 is the main control point; steps with ΔG ≪ 0 are hexokinase, PFK-1 and pyruvate kinase.

steps.title: Phosphorylation
steps.text: Hexokinase adds a phosphate to glucose, trapping it as glucose-6-phosphate (−1 ATP).

steps.title: Isomerisation and second phosphate
steps.text: G6P becomes fructose-6-phosphate; PFK-1 adds a second phosphate (−1 ATP), the committed step.

steps.title: Splitting
steps.text: Aldolase cleaves the six-carbon sugar into two three-carbon sugars.

steps.title: Oxidation
steps.text: G3P is oxidised and phosphorylated, making NADH.

steps.title: Substrate-level phosphorylation
steps.text: Phosphate groups are transferred to ADP, making 4 ATP in all.

steps.title: Pyruvate
steps.text: Pyruvate kinase makes pyruvate, which goes to the mitochondrion or to fermentation.

title: Citric acid cycle (steps)
summary: Eight steps that oxidise acetyl units.

layers.basics: An acetyl group joins a four-carbon molecule to make a six-carbon one. Going round the loop, two carbons leave as CO₂ and the four-carbon starter is rebuilt. The carbons lost in one turn are not the acetyl carbons just added; those leave in later turns.
layers.deeper: Each turn makes 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂ and 1 GTP (or ATP, depending on the tissue).
layers.expert: α-Ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and isocitrate dehydrogenase are key regulated steps.

steps.title: Condensation
steps.text: Acetyl-CoA joins oxaloacetate to make citrate.

steps.title: Isomerisation
steps.text: Citrate is rearranged to isocitrate.

steps.title: First decarboxylation
steps.text: Isocitrate is oxidised to α-ketoglutarate, releasing CO₂ and NADH.

steps.title: Second decarboxylation
steps.text: α-Ketoglutarate is oxidised to succinyl-CoA, releasing CO₂ and NADH.

steps.title: Substrate-level phosphorylation
steps.text: Succinyl-CoA yields succinate and GTP.

steps.title: Regeneration
steps.text: Succinate is oxidised to fumarate (making FADH₂), fumarate is hydrated to malate, and malate is oxidised to oxaloacetate (making NADH), which restarts the cycle.

layers.basics: Electrons from NADH and FADH₂ flow to oxygen, pumping protons that power ATP synthase.
layers.deeper: The proton-motive force, a combined pH difference and voltage across the inner mitochondrial membrane, is the energy store. The total of ≈ 30–32 ATP per glucose counts all stages of respiration; oxidative phosphorylation gives most of it.
layers.expert: ≈ 10 H⁺ pumped per NADH; ≈ 4 H⁺ per ATP including phosphate transport; P/O ≈ 2.5 for NADH (about 2.3 if the ATP synthase needs 10/3 H⁺ per ATP).

steps.title: Electron donation
steps.text: NADH gives electrons to Complex I; FADH₂ gives them to Complex II.

steps.title: Proton pumping
steps.text: Complexes I, III and IV pump protons from matrix to intermembrane space.

steps.title: Carriers
steps.text: Ubiquinone and cytochrome c ferry electrons between complexes.

steps.title: Oxygen reduction
steps.text: Complex IV passes electrons to O₂, making water.

steps.title: Gradient
steps.text: The proton gradient (Δp ≈ 150–200 mV) accumulates.

steps.title: ATP synthesis
steps.text: Protons flow through ATP synthase, driving ADP + Pi → ATP.

layers.basics: Light energy excites electrons in chlorophyll; the electrons make ATP and NADPH and water is split to oxygen.
layers.deeper: Two photosystems work in series in the thylakoid membrane.
layers.expert: The Z-scheme traces the electron path from PSII (P680) through plastoquinone, cytochrome b6f and plastocyanin to PSI (P700) and ferredoxin; the proton gradient it builds drives ATP synthase. The minimum is ≈ 8 photons per O₂: four electrons are removed from two water molecules, and each is lifted once in each photosystem.

steps.title: Light capture
steps.text: Antenna pigments absorb photons and funnel energy to the PSII reaction centre.

steps.title: Water splitting
steps.text: The oxygen-evolving complex splits water, releasing O₂, protons and electrons.

steps.title: Electron transport
steps.text: Electrons travel through plastoquinone and cytochrome b6f, pumping protons into the lumen, then pass to plastocyanin.

steps.title: Second photosystem
steps.text: PSI re-excites the electrons.

steps.title: NADPH formation
steps.text: Ferredoxin and NADP⁺ reductase make NADPH.

steps.title: ATP formation
steps.text: Protons exit via ATP synthase, forming ATP.

layers.basics: Plants attach CO₂ to a five-carbon sugar and reshuffle carbons to make sugar and regenerate the starter.
layers.deeper: Three phases: fixation, reduction and regeneration.
layers.expert: Rubisco catalyses carboxylation of RuBP; the cycle consumes 3 ATP and 2 NADPH per CO₂.

steps.title: Fixation
steps.text: Rubisco joins CO₂ to RuBP, making two 3-phosphoglycerate.

steps.title: Phosphorylation
steps.text: ATP converts 3-PGA to 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate.

steps.title: Reduction
steps.text: NADPH reduces it to glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (G3P).

steps.title: Export
steps.text: One G3P leaves for every three CO₂ fixed.

steps.title: Regeneration
steps.text: The remaining G3P is rearranged to RuBP using ATP.

steps.title: Control
steps.text: Light activates the enzymes through pH, Mg²⁺ and thioredoxin.

title: Meiosis

layers.basics: One diploid cell divides twice to make four haploid cells with new gene combinations.
layers.deeper: Homologues pair and swap pieces in prophase I; sister chromatids separate in meiosis II.
layers.expert: Chiasmata hold homologues together; cohesin protection at centromeres lets sisters stay joined until meiosis II.

facts: ≈ 22–28 per sperm in 20 donors; more in female meiosis

steps.title: Prophase I
steps.text: Homologous chromosomes pair (synapsis) and crossing over occurs.

steps.title: Metaphase I
steps.text: Homologous pairs align at the equator; orientation is random.

steps.title: Anaphase I
steps.text: Homologues are pulled to opposite poles; sisters stay together.

steps.title: Telophase I
steps.text: Two haploid cells form, each with duplicated chromosomes.

steps.title: Meiosis II
steps.text: Sister chromatids separate as in mitosis.

steps.title: Gametes
steps.text: Four genetically distinct haploid cells result.

title: PCR

layers.basics: Heat splits DNA, primers attach, and a polymerase copies the target; repeating doubles the copies each time.
layers.deeper: Each cycle has denaturation, annealing and extension.
layers.expert: Efficiency E < 1 gives N = N₀(1 + E)ⁿ; Taq error ≈ 10⁻⁵–10⁻⁴ per base, higher-fidelity enzymes ≈ 10⁻⁶.

facts: ≤ 2³⁰ ≈ 10⁹ per template, reached only at 100% efficiency; fewer in practice

steps.title: Prepare
steps.text: Mix template DNA, primers, dNTPs, buffer and heat-stable polymerase.

steps.title: Denature
steps.text: Heat to ≈ 95 °C to separate the strands.

steps.title: Anneal
steps.text: Cool to ≈ 55–65 °C so primers bind the target.

steps.title: Extend
steps.text: Heat to ≈ 72 °C; polymerase extends the primers.

steps.title: Repeat
steps.text: 25–35 cycles amplify the target exponentially.

steps.title: Analyse
steps.text: Check product size by gel electrophoresis or measure by qPCR.

title: CRISPR–Cas9 editing

layers.basics: A guide RNA leads Cas9 to a matching site, Cas9 cuts, and the cell's repair changes the gene.
layers.deeper: The edit can disable a gene or insert a new sequence from a template.
layers.expert: Requires a PAM (NGG for SpCas9); NHEJ often leaves small insertions or deletions (indels); HDR efficiency varies widely with cell type, locus and delivery, is usually lower than NHEJ, and needs dividing cells (S/G2 phase).

facts: varies widely with cell type, locus and cell-cycle stage; usually lower than NHEJ
open_questions: How can the outcome of DNA repair after a Cas9 cut be predicted and controlled?
How can off-target edits be measured completely and reduced?
How durable and safe is editing inside the body, over years?

steps.title: Design
steps.text: Choose a 20-nt guide next to a PAM in the target gene.

steps.title: Delivery
steps.text: Deliver Cas9 and guide RNA into cells (plasmid, RNP or viral vector).

steps.title: Target search
steps.text: The Cas9–guide complex scans DNA for the PAM and matching sequence.

steps.title: Cut
steps.text: Cas9 makes a double-strand break 3 bp from the PAM.

steps.title: Repair
steps.text: NHEJ makes small indels; HDR copies a supplied template.

steps.title: Verify
steps.text: Sequence the target and check off-target sites.

title: Viral replication cycle

layers.basics: A virus enters a cell, uses the cell's machinery to copy its genome and proteins, assembles new particles and leaves.
layers.deeper: Lytic viruses burst cells; some viruses bud out; some integrate and hide.
layers.expert: Burst size and the eclipse period (the time before new particles can be detected inside the cell) vary widely between viruses and with host conditions such as temperature and host growth rate; Baltimore class determines the replication strategy.

facts: tens of minutes in E. coli; shorter in faster-growing hosts

steps.title: Attachment
steps.text: Viral proteins bind specific host receptors.

steps.title: Entry
steps.text: The virus enters by fusion or endocytosis and uncoats.

steps.title: Genome replication
steps.text: The genome is copied by viral or host polymerases.

steps.title: Protein synthesis
steps.text: Host ribosomes translate viral mRNA.

steps.title: Assembly
steps.text: Genomes and capsid proteins assemble into virions.

steps.title: Release
steps.text: Virions leave by lysis or budding, infecting new cells.

title: Natural selection

layers.basics: Individuals differ, some differences are inherited, and those that help survival and reproduction become more common.
layers.deeper: Across generations this leads to adaptation to the environment.
layers.expert: For a haploid population in which one type has relative fitness 1 + s and the other 1, with allele frequencies p and q = 1 − p, the change per generation is Δp = s·p·q/w̄, where w̄ = 1 + s·p is the mean fitness. Diploid models add dominance terms. The rate depends on the selection coefficient s and on the variation present.

facts: rose from rare to the large majority in industrial regions during the 1800s, then fell again after clean-air laws

steps.title: Variation
steps.text: Mutation and recombination produce heritable differences.

steps.title: Overproduction
steps.text: In many populations more offspring are born than survive. Selection needs only that individuals differ in how many offspring they leave.

steps.title: Differential survival
steps.text: Individuals with advantageous traits survive and reproduce more.

steps.title: Inheritance
steps.text: Offspring inherit the advantageous alleles.

steps.title: Frequency change
steps.text: The allele becomes more common in the population.

steps.title: Adaptation
steps.text: Over many generations, populations become better suited to the environment.

title: Speciation
summary: How one species splits into two.

layers.basics: Two populations stop, or greatly reduce, exchanging genes and diverge over time. Eventually barriers to interbreeding keep them distinct. These barriers can be partial, and some species still hybridise at low levels.
layers.deeper: A geographic barrier often starts the process.
layers.expert: Reproductive isolation accumulates by Dobzhansky–Muller incompatibilities; reinforcement may strengthen prezygotic barriers in sympatry.

facts: varies from thousands of years to millions, depending on the group
can occur within a single generation
open_questions: How common is speciation with continuing gene flow, compared with speciation in complete isolation?
How often does reinforcement finish the job of reproductive isolation?
Which species concept should be used, given that biologists disagree?

steps.title: Separation
steps.text: A barrier or distance splits a population.

steps.title: Divergence
steps.text: Mutation, drift and selection differ in each group.

steps.title: Local adaptation
steps.text: Each group adapts to its own environment.

steps.title: Isolating barriers
steps.text: Mating-time, behaviour and genetic incompatibilities evolve.

steps.title: Secondary contact
steps.text: If groups meet, hybrids are less fit and mate choice may be reinforced.

steps.title: Two species
steps.text: The groups are now kept distinct by reproductive barriers, which may be partial.

title: Nitrogen cycle
summary: How nitrogen moves between air, soil and life.

layers.basics: Bacteria turn atmospheric nitrogen into forms plants can use, and other bacteria return it to the air.
layers.deeper: Key steps are fixation, nitrification, assimilation, ammonification and denitrification.
layers.expert: Natural biological N fixation is ≈ 200 Tg N/yr (land ≈ 60, range 40–100; ocean ≈ 140 ± 50). Human activity now fixes about as much again, ≈ 210 Tg N/yr for 2010 (Haber–Bosch ≈ 120, nitrogen-fixing crops ≈ 60, fossil-fuel burning ≈ 30). All these global figures are uncertain.

open_questions: How large is nitrogen fixation in the ocean and on land? Current estimates are uncertain by tens of percent.
How big is the nitrous oxide (N₂O) budget, and which sources dominate?
How much do anammox and denitrification each return nitrogen to the air?

steps.title: Fixation
steps.text: Nitrogenase in bacteria (and lightning, industry) converts N₂ to ammonia.

steps.title: Nitrification
steps.text: Soil bacteria oxidise ammonium to nitrite and nitrate.

steps.title: Assimilation
steps.text: Plants take up nitrate or ammonium and build amino acids.

steps.title: Consumption
steps.text: Animals eat plants and obtain nitrogen.

steps.title: Ammonification
steps.text: Decomposers return organic nitrogen as ammonium.

steps.title: Denitrification
steps.text: Anaerobic bacteria convert nitrate back to N₂ (and N₂O).

title: Carbon cycle
summary: Carbon through air, life, ocean and rock.

layers.basics: Plants take CO₂ from the air; respiration, decay and burning return it.
layers.deeper: Oceans and soils store large amounts of carbon, and humans add CO₂ by burning fossil fuels.
layers.expert: Atmosphere ≈ 890 Pg C (2023); fossil fuel emissions ≈ 10 Pg C/yr (2023); land and ocean sinks together absorb roughly half of all emissions.

steps.title: Fixation
steps.text: Photosynthesis converts CO₂ to organic carbon (≈ 120 Pg C/yr on land).

steps.title: Transfer
steps.text: Herbivores and predators pass carbon along food webs.

steps.title: Respiration
steps.text: Organisms oxidise organic carbon and return CO₂.

steps.title: Decomposition
steps.text: Microbes release CO₂ and CH₄ from dead matter.

steps.title: Ocean exchange
steps.text: CO₂ dissolves in seawater; biological pump sinks carbon.

steps.title: Geological exchange
steps.text: Rock weathering, burial of carbonate and organic carbon, and volcanic outgassing move carbon over thousands to millions of years.

steps.title: Human perturbation
steps.text: Fossil fuels and land-use change add CO₂, warming the climate.

title: Signal transduction
summary: From a message arriving at a receptor, on the surface or inside the cell, to a change in what the cell does.

layers.basics: A signal binds a receptor, which passes the message through a chain of molecules to change what the cell does.
layers.deeper: The message is amplified and can be switched off.
layers.expert: Examples: GPCR → G-protein → adenylyl cyclase → cAMP → PKA; RTK → Ras → MAPK cascade → transcription factors.

facts: depends on the pathway; some cascades, such as the visual one, multiply the signal enormously, while others add little gain

steps.title: Reception
steps.text: A ligand binds its receptor.

steps.title: Transduction start
steps.text: The receptor changes shape and activates intracellular proteins such as G proteins or kinases.

steps.title: Second messengers
steps.text: cAMP, Ca²⁺ or IP₃ spread the signal.

steps.title: Kinase cascade
steps.text: Successive phosphorylations amplify the signal.

steps.title: Response
steps.text: Enzymes or transcription factors change cell activity or gene expression.

steps.title: Termination
steps.text: Phosphatases, GTP hydrolysis and phosphodiesterases switch off the signal.

title: How a vaccine builds immunity

layers.basics: A vaccine shows the immune system a harmless form of a pathogen (a weakened or killed whole microbe, a piece of it, or instructions for making a piece) so it can respond quickly later.
layers.deeper: Memory cells and antibodies persist, giving protection.
layers.expert: Primary response ≈ 1–2 weeks; boosters trigger germinal-centre affinity maturation; durability varies from months to decades by antigen.

open_questions: Which immune measurements reliably predict protection for each vaccine?
How long does protection last, and why does it vary so much between vaccines?

steps.title: Antigen delivery
steps.text: The vaccine delivers an antigen or its mRNA.

steps.title: Uptake
steps.text: Dendritic cells take up the antigen and travel to lymph nodes.

steps.title: Presentation
steps.text: Antigen is displayed on MHC to T cells.

steps.title: Activation
steps.text: Helper T cells activate B cells, which make antibodies.

steps.title: Maturation
steps.text: Germinal centres raise antibody affinity.

steps.title: Memory
steps.text: Memory B and T cells persist and respond fast on exposure.

title: Gastrulation

layers.basics: Cells of the early embryo move inward, forming layers that give rise to all tissues.
layers.deeper: In humans the primitive streak marks the start.
layers.expert: Epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, ingression and convergent extension reshape the embryo; Nodal, Wnt and FGF signalling drive it.

facts: about two weeks after fertilisation (varies between embryos)

steps.title: Epiblast and hypoblast
steps.text: The embryo is a two-layered disc.

steps.title: Primitive streak
steps.text: A groove forms along the midline of the epiblast.

steps.title: Ingression
steps.text: Epiblast cells move through the streak.

steps.title: Endoderm and mesoderm
steps.text: Cells that move in first form endoderm; later cells form mesoderm.

steps.title: Ectoderm
steps.text: Cells remaining at the surface form ectoderm.

steps.title: Axis
steps.text: The head–tail, left–right and back–front axes are laid down and patterned during and just after gastrulation.

layers.basics: Sanger sequencing reads one fragment at a time; NGS reads millions to billions in parallel; nanopore sequencing reads single molecules by the change in electrical current as a strand passes through a pore.
layers.deeper: Sanger and Illumina sequencing both use a polymerase and fluorescently labelled bases. Nanopore sequencing needs neither.
layers.expert: Sanger: ddNTP chain termination, capillary electrophoresis; Illumina: bridge amplification and reversible terminators; ONT: current changes through nanopores.

steps.title: Sample preparation
steps.text: DNA is fragmented and adaptors added (NGS) or amplified by PCR (Sanger).

steps.title: Sanger synthesis
steps.text: Chain-terminating ddNTPs with fluorescent tags stop synthesis at each base.

steps.title: Sanger read-out
steps.text: Fragments are separated by size in a capillary and read by laser.

steps.title: NGS clusters
steps.text: Fragments are amplified on a flow cell into clusters.

steps.title: Sequencing by synthesis
steps.text: Fluorescent reversible terminators are imaged base by base.

steps.title: Assembly and analysis
steps.text: Reads are aligned or assembled and variants are called.
